title: Lesson 5: Chords: Open, Barre, Power and Beyond
intro: A chord is a root plus a few intervals (see Chords (#/arts/music-theory/chords) and Roots (#/arts/music-theory/chords/roots)). On the guitar each chord comes as a shape, and the same chord can be voiced in many shapes. This lesson takes you from open chords to barre chords, power chords, small triads and seventh chords.

items: Play the eight open chords and know where each root is.
Play E-shape and A-shape barre chords anywhere on the neck.
Play power chords, three-string triads and shell seventh chords.
Lessons 1–4, especially the note names on strings 6 and 5.

blocks.alt: Eight chord diagrams: C, G, D, A, E, Am, Em and Dm with roots in red.
blocks.caption: The open chords. The red dot or circle is the root; strum from the root string down.

items: Step 1. Step through the open chords below. For each one, find the root (red in the diagram) and strum from that string: C from string 5, G and E from string 6, D from string 4, A and Am from string 5.
Step 2. For each chord, play each string separately: every string should ring clearly. Fix any muted string by arching that finger more.

Step 3. Notice the patterns: E and Em differ by one finger (string 3 fret 1 = G♯ in E, open G in Em): that finger is the third, which makes a chord major or minor. The same is true of A and Am (string 2: C♯ or C).

examples.label: C G D A E Am Em Dm
Major vs minor: E → Em, A → Am

items: Step 1. Play an open E chord with fingers 2, 3 and 4 (instead of 1, 2, 3), leaving finger 1 free.
Step 2. Slide that shape up one fret and lay finger 1 flat across all six strings at fret 1. That is F major (1-3-3-2-1-1): the root F is under finger 1 on string 6.
Step 3. Press with the side of finger 1, close to the fret, and pull the guitar slightly toward you with the fretting arm rather than squeezing harder. Check each string.
Step 4. Move the whole shape: at fret 3 it is G (root G on string 6 fret 3), at fret 5 A, at fret 8 C. The name always comes from the note under finger 1 on string 6.
Step 5. Minor: lift the finger on string 3 (the third): 1-3-3-1-1-1 is F minor. Seventh: from the major shape, lift only the finger on string 4: 1-3-1-2-1-1 is F7.
Step 1. Barre finger 1 across strings 5 to 1 at fret 1, then put fingers 2, 3 and 4 on strings 4, 3 and 2 at fret 3 (or flatten finger 3 across all three): x-1-3-3-3-1 is B♭ major, root on string 5.
Step 3. Move it: at fret 3 it is C, at fret 5 D, at fret 7 E. The name comes from the note under finger 1 on string 5.
Step 4. Between the E shape and the A shape you can now play any major, minor or seventh chord: find its root on string 6 or 5 and put the shape there.

blocks.alt: Six chord diagrams at the first fret: F, Fm and F7 using the E shape with a barre across all six strings, and B♭, B♭m and B♭7 using the A shape with a barre from string 5, roots in red.
blocks.caption: The two barre-chord families. Move any of them along the neck and the red root names the new chord.

examples.label: Moving one shape: G (3), A (5), C (8)

items: Step 1. Put finger 1 on string 6 fret 3 (G) and finger 3 on string 5 fret 5 (D, a fifth above). Strum only those two strings. That is G5, a power chord.
Step 2. Add finger 4 on string 4 fret 5 (G, the octave) for a fuller sound: 3-5-5-x-x-x.
Step 3. Move the shape anywhere on strings 6–5 or 5–4. It has no third, so it is neither major nor minor; that is why it stays clear under heavy distortion.

widget.title: Power chords: G5, A5, C5, D5

blocks.text: Small triads on the top three strings

items: Step 1. Play C major on strings 3, 2 and 1 only: fret 5 on string 3 (C), fret 5 on string 2 (E), fret 3 on string 1 (G). Root position.
Step 2. Move up to x-x-x-9-8-8: E–G–C, first inversion (E is lowest). Then x-x-x-12-13-12: G–C–E, second inversion. All three are C major.
Step 3. These small shapes sound clean in a band and let you play the same chord in three places up the neck.

widget.title: C major triads up the top three strings

items: Step 1. A shell voicing is root, third and seventh: the three notes that define a seventh chord.
Step 2. G7: string 6 fret 3 (G), string 4 fret 3 (F, the seventh), string 3 fret 4 (B, the third): 3-x-3-4-x-x.
Step 3. Cmaj7: string 5 fret 3 (C), string 4 fret 2 (E, third), string 3 fret 4 (B, major seventh): x-3-2-4-x-x.
Step 4. Dm7: x-5-3-5-x-x (D, F, C). Play Dm7 → G7 → Cmaj7: the ii–V–I of jazz, with almost no hand movement.
3 min: open chords, one strum each, saying each root.
4 min: E-shape and A-shape barre chords at three frets each; name the chord from the root.
3 min: power-chord riff G5–A5–C5–D5.
3 min: the three C triads on the top strings, then Dm7–G7–Cmaj7 shells.

blocks.title: Build a barre chord
blocks.text: Play C minor with an E-shape barre and with an A-shape barre.
solution: E shape: root C on string 6 is fret 8: 8-10-10-8-8-8.
A shape: root C on string 5 is fret 3: x-3-5-5-4-3.

blocks.title: Read the voicing
solution: String 5 fret 5 = D; string 4 fret 7 = A; string 3 fret 5 = C; string 2 fret 6 = F. D–A–C–F = root, 5th, 7th, 3rd: D minor seventh (Dm7).

blocks.text: Sources: Greene, T. (1971). Chord Chemistry. Dale Zdenek Publications (later reissued by Alfred); Goodrick, M. (1987). The Advancing Guitarist. Hal Leonard; Leavitt, W. G. (1966–1971). A Modern Method for Guitar, vols. 1–3. Berklee Press; Pass, J. (1986). Joe Pass Guitar Chords. Mel Bay.
